messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Ethan, a 37‑year‑old database administrator from a small town in the Midwest, had always been the steady, quiet type—accurate with his code, meticulous about his meals, and comfortable in the predictability of his work schedule. When he was taken to the emergency department after a sudden collapse, the routine was shattered. He had never before felt so suddenly vulnerable; the bright fluorescent lights of the triage room, the sharp hiss of the oxygen tubing, and the stinging feel of the IV needle as the nurse inserted it were all the more vivid against the backdrop of his fear. The doctors told him he had suffered a massive pulmonary embolism, that a clot had traveled from his leg to his lungs and had nearly ended his life. He was intubated, sedated, and placed on a ventilator for days. The memory of that moment—hands gripping his chest, the taste of antiseptic, the cold metal of the breathing tube—remained as clear and terrifying as if it had happened yesterday. The threat he sensed from that event did not disappear when the tube was removed. Instead, it settled into the muscle of his body, an almost constant tension that made him feel that danger could return at any instant. In the weeks that followed, Ethan noticed that even simple thoughts of “breathing” or “medical procedures” triggered a fluttering in his chest and a racing heart. The threat of a sudden medical crisis had become part of his everyday experience. Because of that persistent sense of threat, he began to adopt a strict eating schedule, believing that controlling his calorie intake would give him a semblance of control over his body’s unpredictable response. The more he restricted his food, the more he felt that his body was constantly on edge, and the fear of the next crisis seemed to grow in tandem with his hunger. This belief—his threat had made him feel that any deviation from control could provoke a life‑threatening event—became the foundation for his maladaptive strategies. His avoidance patterns multiplied. After the ICU stay, the thought of stepping outside for a walk became unbearable. The very idea of exercise was associated with the feeling of breathlessness he had experienced in the hospital; the fear that his heart might surge and he would need to be rushed to the ER again. So he stopped jogging, skipping his morning walks, and even declined to walk with his sister to a grocery store. The avoidance of physical activity not only removed a healthy outlet but also reinforced the body’s sense that it was fragile and unsteady. When he finally did a short stroll around the block, his lungs seemed to protest, his chest tightened, and his breathing felt labored. That experience amplified his threat perception, feeding back into the belief that exercise was dangerous. The avoidance thus kept the loop of threat and fear alive. Ethan also became increasingly cautious about any medical cue. The mere sight of a white coat or the sound of a stethoscope could send a wave of panic through him. The avoidance of hospitals and clinics meant that routine health checks were postponed; his routine blood work and minor vaccinations fell through the cracks. In the workplace, his careful attention to detail made him double‑check everything, but when he accidentally left a database field blank, he would panic, feeling as if the error could cause a catastrophic system failure. The fear of being caught, the anticipation of a negative reaction from colleagues, and the threat of a personal health crisis all converged in this moment, causing his body to shiver, his heart to race, and his thoughts to spiral. This cascade of threat, maladaptive strategy, and trigger solidified the cycle. For months, Ethan’s avoidance and threat perceptions grew. His relationship with his ex‑wife deteriorated because he would not leave the house to meet her, fearing that a health crisis might occur while she was there, and she could be left in a dangerous situation. At work, he missed a critical system upgrade because the prospect of a brief emergency assessment by an IT specialist made him feel that he was inviting a crisis. He found himself constantly scanning his environment for any hint of medical equipment, and his diet had become so restrictive that he began to experience dizziness, which in turn made his breathing feel even more labored. The feedback loop of threat, avoidance, and maladaptive strategy had become a self‑reinforcing spiral. The tipping point came when, during a routine meeting, Ethan felt a tightness in his chest that escalated into a full panic attack. He left the room abruptly, the alarm in his chest growing louder than the voice of his manager. That night, he could not sleep, replaying in his mind the image of the hospital bed, the needle, and the cold, white walls. He realized that his life had become a series of controlled actions and avoided moments, and that he had been living in constant hypervigilance. It was then that he reached out to a therapist, hoping to untangle the web of fear that bound him to his own body. He is most afraid that his avoidance will continue to erode his health and relationships, yet he also holds a quiet hope that, with guidance, he can regain agency over his breathing and his life.
